newsitem.title: slovenia: Slovenia PM says will look for broader government.
newsitem.headline: Slovenia PM says will look for broader government.

text.p: Slovenian prime minister- designate Janez Drnovsek said on Friday he would attempt to form a coalition with one or more right-wing parties following Thursday's rejection of his cabinet line-up by parliament.

"I will try to form a broader coalition," Drnovsek told a news conference, adding he hoped to strike a deal with the People's Party, which "so far has showed interest in participating in the government".

Drnovsek's government, a coalition of his Liberal Democrats with the ex-communist United List of Social Democrats, the pensioners' party Desus and the Nationalist Party, failed to gain parliamentary approval in a secret ballot which yielded an evenly split result of 45 votes against 45.
Drnovsek was thought to command 46 seats in the assembly after the defection of an opposition member last month to secure him the one-vote majority he would have needed.
"If talks (with the rightist parties) are unsuccessful, I will propose a government line-up that will be similar to the one I presented the first time," Drnovsek said.
But Drnovsek added he could not rule out the possibility of early elections, which analysts said would be the most likely result of the current political stalemate in the tiny Alpine republic.

"Yesterday's outcome is another reason for possible early elections ... but those are still far away because of formal procedures according to which they can be called only after three prime minister candidates were unsuccessful," he said.
Analysts said Drnovsek's chances of winning support from the "Spring" alliance of rightist parties remained slim.

The group, which together holds 44 seats, comprises the conservative People's Party, the centre-right Social Democrats and the Christian Democrats. It refused to support Drnovsek's cabinet on Thursday, claiming it would be unable to carry out key tasks such as Slovenia's membership in the European Union or a reform of the ailing pension system.

"At the moment it looks like Drnovsek will have to try to form a government with a majority of just one vote again," Igor Luksic, professor of politics at the Ljubljana Univesity's Faculty of Social Sciences, told Reuters.
"The possibility of premature elections in a year or two has increased," he added.

Drnovsek, who has been acting as prime minister since April 1992, by law has to present a new government line-up within 10 days. If the parliament then fails to approve at least two thirds of his ministerial candidates, President Milan Kucan will have to nominate a new prime minister.

"This has rung in a period of uncertainty. The political situation in Slovenia hampers stability at a time when decisions about Slovenia's membership in NATO and the European Union are being taken," said Drago Lavrencic, a Britain-based Slovenian political analyst.
The ex-Yugoslav republic, which gained its independence in 1991, hopes to join NATO by the year 1999 and the EU by 2001.
